books.section: Topic 8.13 The environment and natural resources from 1968 to 1980

primary_sources: EPA, 'The Birth of EPA' and EPA History 1970-1985 (dates)

source: original; stimulus is a table of federal environmental actions

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from EPA histories: NEPA signed January 1, 1970; EPA opened December 2, 1970; Clean Air Act signed December 1970; Clean Water Act enacted October 18, 1972; Endangered Species Act enacted December 28, 1973; DDT uses cancelled in 1972. Dates verified against EPA, 'The Birth of EPA,' EPA History 1970-1985, and the Duke Nicholas School environmental timeline. Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.13; 5 Steps Ch. 28; Princeton Ch. 12).
stimulus.text:
Major federal environmental actions, 1970-1973:

| Action | Date | What it did |
| National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) | January 1, 1970 | Required federal agencies to assess the environmental effects of their projects |
| Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) | December 2, 1970 | New federal agency to enforce environmental laws |
| Clean Air Act | 1970 | Set national standards for air quality and auto emissions |
| Clean Water Act | October 18, 1972 | Set federal limits on pollutants discharged into waters |
| Endangered Species Act | December 28, 1973 | Protected species at risk of extinction and their habitats |
| DDT ban | December 31, 1972 | EPA ended nearly all uses of the pesticide DDT |

stem: Taken together, the actions in the table best support which conclusion about the early 1970s?

options.text: The federal government ignored pollution until the 1980s.
options.misconception: The table lists six federal actions from 1970 to 1973, the opposite of ignoring pollution.

options.text: Environmental protection became a major federal job.
Congress passed environmental laws only when presidents opposed them.
options.misconception: Background: President Nixon signed these laws and created the EPA, so the laws had presidential support.

options.text: The states took over all environmental enforcement from Washington.
options.misconception: Background: The table shows Washington creating an agency and setting national standards, not handing the job to the states.

rationales.A: The table lists six federal actions from 1970 to 1973, the opposite of ignoring pollution.
rationales.B: Background: In four years Washington created an agency, set national air and water standards, protected endangered species, and banned DDT, a whole new federal job.
rationales.C: Background: President Nixon signed these laws and created the EPA, so the laws had presidential support.
rationales.D: Background: The table shows Washington creating an agency and setting national standards, not handing the job to the states.
rationales.general:
1. The table packs six major actions into four years, 1970 to 1973.
2. Background: They cover air, water, species, and chemicals, so the government took on the whole environment, not one problem.
3. Background: A new agency, the EPA, was created to run that job, which shows it was meant to last.
Remember: When a table shows many actions in a short span, the pattern is the answer.
